resources.string: A calm walk around the house gives the best picture of maintenance and possible major problems.
Walk around the house before going inside | Check that walls stand straight and roof lines run straight | Look for plants growing against walls or on the roof | Take overview photos of every facade
Crooked lines, missing maintenance, damp patches, vegetation and patchwork repairs.
Straight lines, tidy facades, no visible damage.
Sagging ridge, cracks, loose tiles, a lot of deferred maintenance.
Long vacancy, deferred maintenance, structural problems.
Deferred maintenance usually costs more than the asking price suggests.
List everything you notice and then check it point by point.
With crooked lines or large cracks: have a geometra or engineer look at it.
Your nose is a good instrument: musty, mouldy or gas-like smells point to problems.

Smell immediately on entering, before windows are opened | Notice musty air in cellar, cupboards and bedrooms | Notice sewer smells in bathroom and kitchen | Ask whether the house was recently aired or perfumed
Musty air, sewer smell, gas smell, strong air fresheners.
Musty, mouldy or sewer smell; suspiciously strong air fresheners.
Damp, mould, poor ventilation, faulty traps or drains.
Health complaints and hidden damp problems.
Find the source: fix damp, ventilation or drains.
Smell gas? Do not use switches or flames, leave the house and warn the agent.
With a persistent musty smell: have a specialist investigate damp.
Long-empty Italian houses are often unheated and unventilated, causing damp and pipe problems.
Ask how long the house has been empty | Ask when it was last heated | Look for dust, cobwebs, dead insects and water turned off | Check whether meters were read recently
House recently lived in and heated.
Years of vacancy, water and power disconnected.
Hidden frost damage to pipes, damp and mould.
Have pipes and installations tested before buying.
After long vacancy have the installations tested by a professional.
Fresh paint or new plaster can temporarily hide damp patches, cracks or mould.

Notice a strong paint smell and fresh paint on only parts of walls | Look for new paint low on walls and around windows | Inspect walls with raking light from a torch | Ask why and when it was painted
Locally repainted areas, new skirting or panelling.
Evenly aged paintwork or explainable renovation.
Fresh paint only low on walls or on ceiling spots; blisters in new paint.
Cosmetic preparation for sale to hide defects.
Hidden damp or cracks return after purchase.
Measure with a moisture meter; ask questions; possibly a second visit after rain.
A visual check cannot rule out hidden damp.
When in doubt, have a specialist carry out moisture measurements.
Floors that clearly slope can indicate subsidence or sagging beams.
Place a marble on the floor in several rooms | Use a spirit level on floors and window sills | See whether doors swing open or closed by themselves | Look for gaps between floor and skirting
Rolling marble, crooked doors, gaps under skirting.
Level floor; small deviations are normal in old houses.
Clearly sloping or springy floor, new gaps.
Subsidence, sagging timber beams, damaged load-bearing structure.
Have the cause investigated; strengthen beams or repair foundations.
Do not walk on springy or visibly damaged floors.
With a clear slope or springy floor: call an engineer or geometra.
In Italian houses built before 1992 asbestos cement (eternit) occurs in roofs, chimneys, water tanks and pipes.
Look from a distance at corrugated sheets on roofs, sheds and garages | Look for grey water tanks in attic or on the roof | Look for old flue pipes and cement pipes | Photograph without touching
Grey corrugated sheets, cement-like tanks and pipes, weathered surface.
No suspicious materials or proven removal.
Weathered or broken sheets, moss on corrugated sheets.
Building material from before the 1992 ban.
Health risk when damaged; mandatory professional removal.
Survey and removal by a licensed company (bonifica amianto).
Do not touch, break or drill suspicious material.
Always have suspicious material assessed by a licensed specialist.
Moisture can rise from the ground into walls that are not sufficiently protected against ground moisture.

Inspect the lowest 150 cm of the wall | Look for peeling paint and white salt deposits | Check whether plaster is coming loose | Compare different walls | Measure with a suitable moisture meter if possible
A tide mark low on walls that fades upwards.
Dry, even wall base without salts.
Tide mark up to 50-120 cm, salt bands, crumbling plaster.
Missing or failed damp-proof course; poor drainage; ground moisture.
Damage to plaster and timber, mould, cold and unhealthy indoor climate.
Injected damp-proof course, better drainage, renovation plaster.
Visual inspection and simple moisture readings do not give a definitive diagnosis.
Have a damp specialist or geometra determine the cause before making an offer.
Rainwater gets through the outer wall, often on the weather side or at cracks and poor joints.
Look at inner walls on the rain side for stains at any height | Outside, look for cracks, open joints and broken render | Compare with the gutters above
Damp patches that grow after rain, not only near the floor.
Dark stains high on the wall, peeling paint on the weather side.
Cracks, porous render, leaking gutters, missing drip details.
Mould, frost damage to masonry, rotting beam ends.
Repair render, pointing, gutters and sills.
With large stains or rotten timber: have a builder assess the facade.
Warm, humid indoor air condenses on cold surfaces such as corners, windows and thermal bridges.
Look in outer corners, behind cupboards and at ceiling edges | Look for droplets or black dots on windows and frames | Measure temperature and humidity if possible
Stains in cold corners and on windows, especially bedrooms and bathrooms.
Wet windows, black dots in corners, humidity above 70%.
Little ventilation, thermal bridges, no insulation, drying laundry indoors.
Ventilate, insulate, mechanical extraction, solve thermal bridges.
Condensation is often a usage issue but can also indicate poor insulation.
If unsure whether it is condensation or a leak: have a specialist measure.
Mould grows where it stays damp for long. It is always the result of a moisture problem.
Look behind furniture, in cupboards, corners and around windows | Look under sinks and around showers | Look for stains coming through paint
Black or green dots or patches, musty smell.
Large black patches, mould behind furniture or on ceilings.
Condensation, leaks, rising or penetrating damp.
Health risk, especially for children and people with respiratory problems.
Solve the cause, then have the mould removed professionally.
Do not touch mould with bare hands and do not scrape it off.
For large areas: mould and damp survey by a specialist.
White, powdery crusts (efflorescence, salnitro) form when water evaporates from the wall and leaves salts behind.
Look for white fluffy or crusty deposits on walls and floors | Look especially low on walls and in cellars | Notice crumbling plaster around it
White powder or crystals, often in a horizontal band.
Rising or penetrating damp, salts in old building materials.
Salts keep attracting moisture and destroy plaster and paint.
Address the moisture source, desalinate, apply renovation plaster.
Salt on the wall is a signal, not a diagnosis of the cause.
With extensive salt damage have a specialist find the moisture source.
Paint that peels or blisters shows moisture behind it or the wrong type of paint.
Look for flakes, blisters and loose paint | Press gently on blisters: crunchy powder suggests salt | Note height and location of the damage
Large peeling areas, powder behind the paint.
Damp, salts, non-breathable paint on old walls.
Cosmetic damage and a sign of a moisture source.
Fix the source, then use breathable lime or silicate paint.
If damage keeps returning: damp investigation.
Plaster can come loose because of damp, salts or age. Hollow-sounding plaster is a sign.
Tap gently with a knuckle on suspicious spots | Listen for a hollow sound | Look for bulges and cracks in the plaster
Large hollow areas or pieces already fallen.
Remove loose parts and re-plaster with suitable material.
Do not pull or break pieces off without the owner\'s permission.
With hollow ceiling plaster: have a professional assess safety.
A musty smell in one room helps locate the moisture source.
Smell each room separately, including cupboards and under stairs | Note where the smell is strongest | Combine with moisture readings there
Rooms with a musty or earthy smell.
Strong musty smell in cellar, bedroom or cupboard.
Hidden damp, mould behind finishes, poor ventilation.
Find the moisture source and improve ventilation.
With a strong smell but no visible cause: have a specialist search.
Leaks from the roof cause stains on top-floor ceilings and in the attic.
Check top-floor ceilings for rings and stains | In the attic (only from a safe floor) look for wet spots and water marks on timber | Look around chimneys and roof windows
Yellow/brown rings, discoloured timber, drip marks.
Wet or soft spots, buckets in the attic, fresh stains.
Broken or shifted tiles, poor flashing at chimneys.
Rotting beams, mould, damage to installations.
Repair tiles and flashing, renew underlay.
Never climb onto the roof yourself; look from the ground with binoculars.
Have a roofer or geometra assess the roof if there are stains.
Leaking pipes cause local wet spots, often under or next to kitchen and bathroom.
Look under sinks and washbasins | Look at ceilings below bathrooms | Look along pipe routes in walls and floors
Wet spots not related to rain, limescale on pipes.
Drips, rot in kitchen cabinets, stains below the bathroom.
Old galvanised pipes, leaking joints, frost damage.
Water damage, mould, high water bill.
Locate the leak and replace the pipe.
If a leak in walls is suspected: leak detection by a plumber.
A leaking or blocked downpipe sends water down the facade, causing damp patches inside.
Follow each downpipe from gutter to ground | Look for green stains, algae or damp streaks beside the pipe | Check inside behind that spot for stains
Streaks, moss or discoloration along the pipe.
Wet inner wall at the height of a leaking joint.
Repair or replace the pipe, check the discharge to the drain.
Cellars of old houses are often damp; the question is how severe and whether it is stable.
Smell and look for wet floors, puddles and water lines | Notice rust on metal parts and rotten timber | Measure humidity if possible
Standing water, signs of flooding, sump pits.
With water in the cellar: drainage and groundwater investigation.
Garages against a slope or partly underground often have damp problems.
Look at wet walls on the slope side | Look for water lines and sand on the floor | Check whether there is a floor drain
Water coming in under the door or through the wall.
Puddles, silt on the floor, wet back wall.
Driveway sloping towards the garage, no channel drain, soil against the wall.
Channel drain at the door, drainage behind the wall.
Soil or groundwater against outer walls
If the ground outside is higher than the floor inside, moisture presses directly against the wall.
Compare outside ground level with the inside floor | See whether walls are dug into the hillside | Look for damp inside on those walls
Ground higher than inside floor, wet walls on that side.
Ground lower than the floor and sloping away from the house.
Buried walls without drainage or ventilated cavity (intercapedine).
Building against a slope, raised ground.
Permanently damp walls, mould, health complaints.
Have a geometra assess whether drainage or excavation is possible.
With houses against a slope, rain and groundwater flow towards the house.
See where water from the slope goes when it rains | Look for ditches, channels and drainage above the house | Check the uphill side inside for damp
Water and mud towards the house, wet uphill side.
Water is collected above the house and diverted.
No drainage, traces of mud flows, wet back walls.
Damp problems, pressure on walls, in severe cases instability.
Drainage channels, drains, retaining wall with drainage.
A visual check does not prove there is no landslide risk.
Consult official hazard maps (PAI) and a geologist or geometra.
Water standing along the facade soaks into foundations and walls.
Check that the ground slopes away from the house | Look for puddles, mud and algae along the walls | See where downpipes discharge
Puddles and wet strips along the facade.
Ground slopes away, paving with a channel.
Downpipes discharging onto the ground next to the wall.
No fall, sunken paving, missing channels.
Create a fall, drainage pipe, connect downpipes.
Moisture reading on recently painted walls
On freshly painted spots damp cannot be seen, but it can often be measured.
Measure on the new paint and on an old dry wall as reference | Measure at several heights | Record the values in the moisture module
Clearly higher readings on repainted spots.
Higher readings low on walls or around windows behind fresh paint.
Only compare readings taken with the same device on the same material.
With unusual readings: damp investigation by a specialist.
Behind wardrobes against outer walls the wall is cold and air is still: ideal for mould.
Ask permission to move a cupboard slightly or look with a torch | Look behind beds and sofas against outer walls | Look for mould on the back of furniture
Mould or wet wallpaper behind furniture.
Cold outer wall, condensation, no air circulation.
Insulate, keep furniture away from the wall, ventilate.
Do not move heavy furniture without permission and help.
Leaks, thermal bridges and condensation all come together around windows.
Look under sills and in the corners of the reveals | Look for stains on the wall below the window | Outside, check the sill and sealant joints
Stains, mould or peeling paint around the frame.
Wet plaster under the window, rot in the frame.
Leaking joint, missing drip sill, condensation on single glazing.
Reseal joints, fit a drip sill, repair or replace the frame.
Stains on ceilings come from roof leaks, leaking pipes or bathrooms above, or condensation.
Inspect each ceiling with raking light | Check what is above: roof, bathroom, terrace or pipe | Look for sagging and peeling plaster
Wet or sagging ceiling parts, rust at beams.
Leak from above, terrace without proper waterproofing, condensation.
Repair the source, restore ceiling and if needed beams.
Do not stand under sagging ceiling parts.
With sagging or wet timber: structural assessment.
Timber that stays wet for long rots. Beam ends in walls, frames and roof timbers are especially vulnerable.
Look for dark, cracked or crumbly timber | Look for fungal strands and mushroom-like growth | Look at beam ends in outer walls
Cube-shaped cracking, soft or discoloured wood.
Crumbly wood, fungal strands, sagging beams.
Long-term damp from leaks or poor ventilation.
Loss of strength of beams and floors.
Replace or strengthen affected timber, fix the moisture source.
Do not probe wood without permission; do not walk on affected floors.
With rot in load-bearing timber: call an engineer or carpenter.
The bottom of the walls reveals subsidence or foundation problems.
Walk around and inspect the wall base | Look for cracks that are wider at the bottom | Look for washed-out soil or voids under the wall
Cracks at the base, washed-out soil, tilting.
Wide cracks at the bottom, visible voids, sinking corners.
Subsidence of walls and serious damage.
Do not dig along the foundation.
With signs of subsidence: call an engineer or geologist.
Doors and windows that stick or have slanted gaps may indicate deformation of the building.
Open and close all doors and windows | See whether gaps above doors are slanted | Notice doors that have been planed down
Slanted gaps, planed doors, sticking windows.
Several sticking doors on one side of the house.
Settlement, sagging lintels or floors, damp timber.
Have the cause determined before planing.
With several sticking doors plus cracks: structural assessment.
Roots of large trees close to the house can damage foundations and pipes.
Note trees within about 10 m of the facade | Look for lifted paving | Look for cracks on the tree side
Large trees right next to the house, lifted tiles.
Cracks on the tree side, roots in manholes.
Root growth, drying out of clay soil.
Root barrier, pruning or removal (with permit if required).
Most of Italy is an earthquake area. Older houses often have little or no strengthening.
Ask about the municipality\'s seismic zone and strengthening works carried out | Look for tie plates (capochiave) on the facade | Ask for documentation and permits
Tie plates, ring beams, documented strengthening.
No strengthening, previous earthquake damage, works without permits.
Year of construction, regional building methods.
Vulnerability in earthquakes and higher renovation costs.
Seismic upgrade, possibly with Sismabonus incentives.
Have an engineer assess seismic vulnerability.
Load-bearing walls keep the house standing. Bulging, leaning or removed parts are serious.
Sight along walls to see whether they are straight and plumb | Look for bulges and large cracks | Ask whether walls have been removed
Bulging or leaning walls, large cracks, openings.
Bulging, vertical cracks at corners, removed walls without a beam.
Do not enter spaces with visibly unstable walls.
When in doubt always call an engineer.
Many old Italian houses have timber beam floors or vaults. Sagging and decay matter.
Look at beams and ceilings from below | Walk on the floor (only where safe) and feel whether it is springy | Look for sagging and cracks in beams
Strongly sagging or cracked beams, props.
Risk of collapse in severe cases.
Strengthen or replace beams, concrete topping (soletta collaborante).
Do not walk on springy floors or floors supported by props.
Beetle larvae (tarli) and termites eat timber from the inside.
Look for small round holes in beams, doors and furniture | Look for small piles of fine wood dust below the holes | Look for termite tunnels on walls
Holes of 1-3 mm, fresh wood dust.
No holes or only old, treated infestation.
Fresh dust, many holes in load-bearing beams.
Treatment by a specialist, replace affected parts.
With infestation of load-bearing timber: assessment by a specialist.
Stone vaults (volte) and arches are strong as long as the shape is intact and the walls do not spread.
Look for cracks along the crown of the vault | See whether supporting walls lean outwards | Look for loose stones
Cracks along the vault, spreading walls.
Continuous cracks, sagging crown, loose stones.
Spreading walls, missing tie rods, load above.
Risk of collapse with severe deformation.
Tie rods, lime mortar consolidation, strengthening.
Do not stand under vaults with loose stones.
With cracks in vaults: structural assessment.
Stairs must be solid, safe and comfortable to use.
Walk up and down calmly | Look for loose treads, cracks and wobbly handrails | Look at the support under the stairs
Solid stairs with a good handrail.
Moving or broken treads, cracked stone stairs.
Do not use stairs that move or are damaged.
Later extensions and openings are often built without calculations or permits.
Ask which alterations were done and when | Look where old and new parts meet | Compare the layout with the floor plan (planimetria)
Cracks at junctions, different materials, flat roofs on extensions.
Extensions without permit, openings in load-bearing walls.
Legal problems (abuso edilizio) and structural risks.
Have a geometra check legality and an engineer the structure.
Slanting cracks, or stepped through the joints, often indicate uneven settlement.
Record each crack in the crack module with length and width | See whether the crack is wider at one end | See whether it is visible inside and outside
Slanting crack from corners or openings, stepped pattern in masonry.
At most hairline cracks in plaster.
Cracks wider than a few mm, fresh edges, offset of the wall plane.
Investigate the cause, repair foundations, stitch cracks.
Crack width alone is not enough to judge severity.
Always have diagonal cracks assessed by an engineer.
Horizontal cracks can indicate lateral pressure (soil, roof thrust) or rusting steel.
Look for horizontal cracks in walls, especially against slopes and under eaves | See whether the wall bulges above or below the crack | Measure and record width and length
Long cracks with bulging, cracks under the eaves.
Earth pressure, roof thrust, rusting reinforcement or lintels.
Crack width alone is not enough to judge severity.
Have horizontal cracks with bulging assessed promptly.
Vertical cracks come from shrinkage, temperature or walls separating at corners.
Look for vertical cracks in walls and at corners where walls meet | See whether the crack runs through the whole wall | Record length and width
Straight vertical crack, often at junctions.
Hairline cracks in plaster from shrinkage.
Shrinkage, missing bond between walls, settlement.
Crack width alone is not enough to judge severity.
With through-cracks at corners: structural assessment.
Cracks from the corners of windows and doors indicate weak lintels or settlement.
Inspect all corners of windows and doors inside and outside | See whether the lintel above the opening sags | Record cracks in the crack module
Slanting cracks from corners, sagging lintel.
Wide cracks, displaced stones above the opening.
Weak or rusted lintel, settlement, new opening.
Instability of the masonry above the opening.
Replace or strengthen the lintel, repair the crack.
Crack width alone is not enough to judge severity.
Ceiling cracks can be harmless (plaster) or point to sagging floors.
Inspect ceilings with raking light | Look for cracks along beams and mid-span | Combine with a floor check above
Cracks along beams, sag at mid-span.
Wide cracks with sagging or damp marks.
Do not stand under sagging ceilings.
Cracks in the visible part of the foundation or masonry plinth are an important signal.
Inspect the plinth around the house and in the cellar | Look for cracks that continue into the wall above | Record them in the crack module
Cracks in the plinth running upwards.
Wide or offset cracks, loose stones.
Crack width alone is not enough to judge severity.
Always have them assessed by an engineer.
Facade cracks let water in and can indicate building movement.
Inspect each facade from a distance and up close | Distinguish render crazing (net pattern) from cracks through masonry | Record the largest cracks
Net-like hairline cracks or continuous cracks.
Repair cracks, renew render, address the cause.
Crack width alone is not enough to judge severity.
With continuous cracks: call an engineer.
Cracked tiles in a line can indicate settlement of the subfloor or floor.
See whether broken tiles form a continuous line | Tap tiles: a hollow sound means debonding | Combine with the marble test
Continuous crack line through several tiles.
Crack line plus slope or settlement.
Settlement, sagging, damp under the floor.
With a crack line and slope: structural assessment.
Stone and brick with poor joints let water and frost in.
Inspect joints and stones | Look for eroded joints and loose stones | Notice plants in joints
Recessed joints, loose or spalling stones.
Large areas of eroded joints or loose stones.
Age, frost, cement pointing on soft stone.
Repoint with lime mortar, replace stones.
With loose stones high up: have a builder check.
External render protects the wall; loose render lets rain through.
Inspect render from afar and up close | Tap gently on low parts: hollow = loose | Look for fallen pieces
Large loose areas, especially on the weather side.
Local repair or complete new render.
Loose render high up can fall: do not stand underneath.
Thick stone walls store heat and coolness but are hard to insulate and may hold moisture.
Measure wall thickness at a window or door | Note the material (stone, brick, concrete) | Ask about later insulation
Thickness and material of outer walls.
Thin walls without insulation, or mixed materials.
Affects comfort, energy use and moisture behaviour.
Internal or external insulation (cappotto) with breathable materials.
Climbing plants and vegetation on walls
Ivy and rooting plants keep walls wet and penetrate joints.
Look for ivy, shrubs in walls and growth against the facade | Look for roots in joints and eaves
Shrubs growing out of the wall, ivy up to the roof.
Projecting concrete edges and cornices can crumble and fall.
Look at the underside of balconies and cornices | Look for rusting reinforcement and spalled concrete | Notice safety nets or barriers
Brown rust stains, exposed rebar, spalled edges.
Do not stand under damaged balconies.
With exposed rebar: call a builder or engineer.
The facade finish reveals maintenance; a new facade can also hide things.
Look for discoloration, peeling and algae | Ask when the facade was refurbished | Notice recent local repairs
Large weathered areas, local fresh patches.
Facade refurbishment costs, possibly hidden defects.
In terraced or village houses, the state of the neighbours affects your house.
Look at the condition of adjoining buildings | Ask whether the neighbouring house is empty or derelict | Look for cracks at the junction
Derelict neighbour, cracks at the party wall.
Collapsing or empty neighbouring building, damp from the neighbours.
Damp, structural risk and maintenance disputes.
With a derelict neighbour: have a geometra assess the risks.
Shifted, broken or missing tiles are the biggest source of roof leaks.
Inspect the roof with binoculars from several sides | Look for gaps, shifted tiles and moss | Notice wavy roof lines
Broken or shifted tiles, moss, plants.
Gaps, missing tiles, sagging roof plane.
Relay tiles (ripassatura) or renew the roof with underlay.
Never climb onto the roof; look from the ground, a window or a safe spot with binoculars.
Have a roofer assess the condition.
A sagging ridge indicates weak or rotten roof timber or spreading walls.
Check from a distance whether the ridge is straight | See whether roof planes are dished | Combine with attic inspection
Clear sagging, cracks under the eaves.
Risk of collapse and high costs.
Repair or renew roof structure, ring beam (cordolo).
Never climb onto the roof; look from the ground, a window or a safe spot with binoculars.
Chimneys often leak, and old chimneys can be unstable.
Inspect chimneys with binoculars | Look for leaning, loose bricks and missing cap | Inside, look for stains around the flue
Leaning or cracked chimney, stains around it.
Loose bricks, leaning, wet spots at the chimney.
Never climb onto the roof; look from the ground, a window or a safe spot with binoculars.
Timber eaves and fascia boards rot when water stands on them for long.
Look at the underside of the eaves | Notice rot, loose boards and missing pieces | Look for damp marks on the facade below
Rotten timber, loose parts, stains below.
Never climb onto the roof; look from the ground, a window or a safe spot with binoculars.
Flat roofs and terraces over living space often leak due to worn waterproofing.
Look (if safely accessible) for puddles and cracks | Look at the outlets | Check ceilings below
Stains on the ceiling below, blocked outlet.
Only step onto roofs with a safe parapet.
Age and history of the roof
The age of the roof largely determines future costs.
Ask when the roof was renewed or relaid | Ask for invoices and guarantees | Ask whether there is insulation and underlay
Year of last renovation, insulation, underlay.
Roof older than 40-50 years without maintenance.
Large investment in the short term.
Plan and budget a roof renovation.
Roof window junctions are vulnerable to leaks.
Inside, look for stains around roof windows | Open and close the roof window | Notice condensation and rot
Stains around the window, rotten frame.
Gutters collect roof water; leaking or blocked gutters damage the facade.
Follow the gutters with binoculars | Look for sagging, rust, holes and plants | Look for streaks on the facade below
Holes, loose brackets, water spilling over.
Never climb onto the roof; look from the ground, a window or a safe spot with binoculars.
Many old houses have no gutters: water falls straight down the wall onto the ground.
Check whether all eaves have a gutter | Look for washed-out soil under the eaves | Notice wet wall bases
Gutters on all eaves or a wide overhang.
Wet walls and washout along the foundation.
Damp in walls and foundation damage.
Overflowing gutters leave black or green streaks and moss on the facade.
Look for vertical streaks below the gutter | Look for moss on the facade | Ask when gutters were last cleaned
Streaks and algae under the gutter.
Wide wet strips, inside stains at the same spot.
Downpipes discharging next to the wall flood the foundation.
Follow every downpipe to its end | See whether it connects to a drain, pit or channel | Notice wet spots at the outlet
Discharge onto the ground next to the wall.
Connected to a drain or far from the house.
Puddles and wet wall base at the outlet.
Dented, broken or loose pipes leak water against the facade.
Inspect all joints and brackets | Look for cracks and rust | Notice missing parts
Pipe broken off halfway down the facade.
Single glazing means cold, condensation and high heating costs. Costs are per window.
Look at the edge of the glass: double glazing has a spacer | Hold a light in front of the glass: two reflections = double glazing | Count windows with single glazing
Single glazing, misted double glazing (failed seal).
Double glazing without condensation between panes.
Single glazing in many windows, condensation between panes.
Windows must open, close and lock properly.
Open and close each window | Check locks and hinges | Feel for draughts when closed
Windows that cannot open or close.
Shutters protect against sun, intrusion and weather; broken shutters are a significant cost.
Open and close shutters and roller shutters | Look for rot, rust and broken slats | Check straps and motors
Rotten wood, broken slats, stuck roller shutters.
Low parapets and missing railings are a fall risk; bars can block escape routes.
Check the height of parapets at windows and stairs | See whether bars can be opened from inside | Look for unstable railings
Loose railings or no fall protection.
Fit or raise railings, lockable bars.
Timber frames rot mostly at the bottom and in corners.
Look at sills and corners | Press gently with a finger (do not probe without permission) | Notice peeling paint and open joints
Soft or discoloured wood, open joints.
Open sealant joints between frame and wall let rain and draughts in.
Look inside and outside along the frame | Look for cracks and missing sealant | Notice stains in the reveal
Timber, aluminium without thermal break or PVC determine comfort and maintenance.
Note the frame material | Ask the year of installation | Notice cold aluminium profiles with condensation
Old non-insulated aluminium, decayed timber frames.
The front door determines security, insulation and weather-tightness.
Open, close and lock the door | Look at the bottom and threshold for rot or rust | Ask about the lock type (porta blindata?)
Sticking, draughts, rotten bottom, basic lock.
Solid, tight door with a good lock.
Rot, poor closing, water under the door.
Repair or replace with a security door.
Interior doors reveal building deformation and the general finish.
Open and close all interior doors | Notice slanted gaps and planed parts | See whether doors move by themselves
Many crooked doors on one side.
Possible sign of movement; finishing costs.
Heavy garage doors and gates must operate safely.
Operate the garage door and any gate | Notice rust, misalignment and safety devices on electric doors | Ask about remote controls
Rust, heavy operation, missing safety devices.
Broken springs, door that drops, faulty motor.
Never stand under a moving door.
A modern board has an RCD (salvavita) and circuit breakers instead of fuses.
Look at the board from the outside only | Look for an RCD with a test button | Notice porcelain fuses and loose wires
Rewirable fuses, no RCD, scorch marks.
Closed board with RCD and breakers.
Exposed wiring, scorch marks, improvised fuses.
Renew the board by a licensed electrician.
Never open the consumer unit, distribution board or sockets, and do not touch live parts.
Always have the installation checked by a licensed electrician.
Old wiring (fabric cables, surface conduits, no earth) usually needs complete replacement.
Look at visible cables and switches | Notice two-pin sockets without earth | Ask the year of the last renewal
Fabric cables, porcelain switches, surface wiring.
Mixed old and new parts, loose cables.
Never open the consumer unit, distribution board or sockets, and do not touch live parts.
Have an electrician assess the condition.
A plug-in tester shows whether there is earth without opening anything (only with permission).
Count the sockets per room | Use a plug-in tester with permission if you have one | Notice discoloured or loose sockets
Hot spots, loose or damaged sockets.
Never open the consumer unit, distribution board or sockets, and do not touch live parts.
Installations after 1990 should have a Dichiarazione di conformità (DiCo); otherwise a Dichiarazione di rispondenza.
Ask for the DiCo or DiRi | Ask who installed the system | Record the answer in the documents module
No certificate or altered installation without a new one.
Inspection and new certificate by a licensed installer.
In Italy 3 kW is standard; a heat pump, induction hob or EV charger often needs more.
Ask the contracted power (kW) | Ask whether the connection is active | See where the meter is
Disconnected supply, 3 kW with electric cooking and heating.
Request a power upgrade from the grid operator.
Look at outdoor lights, sockets and cables in the garden | Notice loose cables and open boxes | Ask whether garden lighting works
Loose cables, open boxes, improvised extensions.
Cables on the ground, damaged boxes.
Have it renewed by an installer.
Never open the consumer unit, distribution board or sockets, and do not touch live parts.
Is there mains water (acquedotto), a private well or a tank? That determines quality and reliability.
Ask where the water comes from | Ask about shortages in summer | With permission, run a tap and notice colour and pressure
No connection, cloudy water, summer shortages.
Connect, filter, storage tank or pump.
Have well water analysed before drinking it.
Old galvanised steel pipes rust up; lead pipes are unhealthy.
Look at visible pipes under the sink and at the meter | Notice rust and scale | Ask about renewal
Grey galvanised or lead pipes, rust marks.
Leaks and low pressure; lead is unhealthy.
Test pressure and drainage by (with permission) opening several taps at once.
With permission, open a tap upstairs and downstairs at the same time | Flush the toilet | See how fast water drains
Hardly any pressure upstairs, gurgling drains.
Scale, rust, blockage, low mains pressure.
Booster pump, clean or replace pipes.
In mountain villages pipes freeze in unheated spaces and outer walls.
See whether pipes run through unheated spaces or outside | Ask whether the house is drained in winter | Look for repaired or split pipes
Unprotected pipes in cellar, garage or outside.
Split pipes, signs of frozen water.
Not every Italian house is connected to the public sewer (fognatura).
Ask whether the house is connected to the fognatura | Ask about a septic tank or treatment system | Look for manhole covers around the house
Discharge into soil or stream without permit.
Connect or install a permitted treatment system.
Sewer smell and slow drainage point to blockages, missing venting or dry traps.
With permission, run water in sink, shower and toilet | Smell at gullies and drains | Listen for gurgling
Water coming back up, wet spots at manholes.
With recurring problems: CCTV survey of the drains.
Manholes must be accessible and not flooded.
Find manhole covers around the house | Look (without forcing covers) for signs of overflow | Ask where the main drain runs
Do not lift heavy covers or enter manholes.
A septic tank (fossa settica/Imhoff) must be well located, accessible and permitted.
Ask where the tank is and what type | Ask for the discharge permit (autorizzazione allo scarico) | See whether a tanker can reach it
Unknown location, no permit, tank close to a well.
Obtain a permit or install a new system.
Do not open a septic tank or lean over an open pit: toxic gases.
Have the system assessed by a specialist.
A septic tank must be emptied regularly.
Ask when the tank was last emptied | Ask for invoices | Smell around the tank
Do not open a septic tank or lean over an open pit: toxic gases.
The treated water often goes into the ground via a dispersal field (subirrigazione).
Ask where the field is | Look for unusually green, wet or smelly areas | Note distance to wells and slopes
Wet, smelly or extra green patches.
New dispersal field or treatment system.
Do not open a septic tank or lean over an open pit: toxic gases.
Many Italian houses only have a stove, pellet or wood burner, or an old boiler.
Note the heating system and fuel | Ask about age and maintenance (libretto impianto) | Ask whether all rooms are heated
No central heating, stove only, old boiler.
New boiler, heat pump or pellet system.
Note age, location and service records of the boiler.
Read the rating plate and year without opening the boiler | Ask for the libretto and last check | Notice soot marks and leaks
Boiler under 15 years with recent service.
Soot, leaks, open-flued boiler in living space.
Do not open the boiler or touch gas parts.
Have the boiler checked by a licensed installer.
Radiators show whether the system is well maintained.
Look for rust and leaks at valves | Ask whether all radiators heat up | Note rooms without a radiator
Wood stove, pellet stove and fireplace
Stoves and fireplaces need a sound flue and regular sweeping.
Inspect the stove and flue | Notice soot marks, cracks and discoloured ceiling | Ask when the flue was swept
Soot marks, cracks, discoloration around the flue.
Smoke in the room, charred beams near the flue.
Sweep, inspect and line the flue.
Have a chimney specialist (fumista) check the flue.
Ask for actual annual costs; they say more than the energy label.
Ask for bills for gas, LPG, wood or pellets | Ask how many rooms were heated | Note the amounts
Very high costs or no information.
Hot water comes from a combi boiler, electric water heater, solar or heat pump cylinder.
Ask which system is installed | With permission, run hot water and time how quickly it heats | Look at age and scale
Quick hot water from a recent system.
Long waits, leaking cylinder, rusty water.
Replace heater, possibly a heat pump cylinder.
Solar systems save a lot, but only if they work and are maintained.
Ask whether there are solar collectors or PV panels and whether they work | Ask about age, maintenance and contracts (GSE) | Inspect from a distance for damage
Faulty panels, leaking collectors, unclear contracts.
Have it checked, take over contracts.
Location and condition of the water heater
A leaking cylinder in an attic or cupboard can cause major damage.
Find the water heater or cylinder | Notice rust, leaks and a missing relief valve drain | Look for stains below
Rust, leaks, no relief valve drain.
Rust stains and water under the cylinder.
Gas comes from the mains (metano), an LPG tank in the garden or bottles.
Ask which gas and whether the tank is rented or owned | See where bottles and tank are | Ask about inspections
Type of gas, tank ownership, bottle location.
Gas bottles indoors in cupboards, rusty tank, unclear contracts.
Take over or replace the tank, move bottles outside.
Do not dismantle anything on the gas installation. If you smell gas: no switches or flames, go outside and warn the agent.
Have the gas installation inspected by a licensed installer.
Gas appliances in a room require a permanent vent; hoses have an expiry date.
Look at the gas hose behind the cooker (expiry date printed on it) | Find the vent in the kitchen or boiler room wall | Notice taped-over grilles
Expired hoses, covered or missing ventilation.
Gas leak and carbon monoxide risk.
Do not dismantle anything on the gas installation. If you smell gas: no switches or flames, go outside and warn the agent.
The gas installation should also have a Dichiarazione di conformità.
Ask for the certificate and installation year | Ask about the last inspection | Record it in the documents module
No certificate or old installation without checks.
Yellow flames, soot and discoloration indicate poor combustion and CO risk.
Look (only if the owner lights the hob) at flame colour | Look for soot above appliances | Ask about a CO alarm
Soot on walls, occupants feeling sick.
Do not dismantle anything on the gas installation. If you smell gas: no switches or flames, go outside and warn the agent.
Most heat is lost through an uninsulated roof, and the house overheats in summer.
Ask whether the roof is insulated | Look in the attic (safely) for insulation | In summer, feel whether the top floor is very hot
No insulation, damaged or wet insulation.
Do not touch old insulation or boards (possible asbestos).
Old stone walls are rarely insulated; external insulation (cappotto) is expensive but effective.
Ask whether walls are insulated | Look at window depth (thick layer may mean cappotto) | Feel whether outer walls are cold
Uninsulated thin walls, mould on walls.
Cappotto or internal insulation with breathable materials.
Floor insulation above cellar or ground
Cold floors above a cellar, garage or directly on the ground reduce comfort.
Feel whether the floor is cold | From the cellar, look for insulation under the floor | Ask about the floor build-up
Cold floor, damp in the floor.
Floor on the ground without insulation or damp barrier.
Insulate below the floor or new ventilated floor (vespaio).
The APE certificate is mandatory for sale and gives the energy class (A4 to G).
Request the APE | Check that it is valid (10 years) and matches the current situation | Note class and consumption
Class and consumption in kWh/m² per year.
Valid APE that matches the house.
No APE, expired or clearly wrong.
Have an APE drawn up by a certifier.
Real bills for electricity, gas and fuel give the best picture.
Ask for bills of the last 12 months | Ask how the house was used (permanent or holiday) | Note annual totals
No data or holiday use only.
Make your own estimate with an installer.
The position relative to the sun determines warmth, light and solar potential.
Use a compass app to determine orientation of living room and roof | See whether mountains or trees block winter sun | Ask how many hours of sun there are in winter
Location in a valley or on a north slope.
Colder, damper house and less solar energy.
Without good ventilation moisture stays in the house.
Check for vents or extraction | Measure humidity in several rooms | Notice misted windows
No vents, high RH, misted windows.
Closed-up house, new airtight windows without ventilation.
Bathrooms without a window must have working extraction.
Check whether bathroom and kitchen have a window or extractor | Have the extractor switched on | Notice mould on the ceiling
Replacing a kitchen is a major cost; look at cabinets, worktop and appliances.
Open cupboards and drawers | Look under the sink for leaks and rot | Ask which appliances stay and whether they work
Rot under the sink, broken cupboards, old appliances.
Water damage, mould, appliances not working.
Gas or electric cooking determines ventilation requirements and power supply.
See whether there is gas or induction | See whether the hood vents outside | Check the vent opening with gas
Recirculating hood without ventilation with gas, grease build-up.
Hood vented outside and vent opening.
No vent opening with gas cooking.
Loose tiles and open joints behind the worktop let water into the wall.
Tap tiles behind the worktop | Check sealant around the sink | Notice swelling of the worktop
Hollow tiles, open joints, swollen worktop.
Showers and baths often leak through joints and sealant into rooms below.
Look at sealant and joints at shower and bath | Tap tiles: hollow = loose | Look at the ceiling below
Black sealant, open joints, loose tiles, stains below.
Wet walls around the shower, stains on the ceiling below.
Reseal, regrout, waterproofing or new bathroom.
Old fixtures and taps cause leaks and limescale problems.
Flush the toilet and check whether it keeps running | Open taps (with permission) | Look for cracks in basin and toilet
Bathrooms without ventilation almost always have mould.
Look at ceiling and corners | Check window or extractor | Notice peeling paint
Lots of mould, no window or extractor.
An extra or renovated bathroom is a common and costly wish.
Count bathrooms and toilets | See whether the layout is practical | Ask whether bathrooms in extensions are permitted
One small outdated bathroom, bathroom in an illegal extension.
Living room: light, space and layout
The living room is the main living space; light and layout are hard to change.
Assess daylight and view | Roughly measure the room | Notice fireplace, ceiling height and beams
Dark room, low ceilings, awkward layout.
In Italy 2.70 m is usually the minimum height for living spaces; lower rooms are officially not habitable.
Measure ceiling height in living spaces | Compare with the official use on the floor plan | Notice attics used as bedrooms
Bedrooms in attic or cellar below minimum height.
Room does not legally count as living space.
Check with a geometra; possibly change the use.
Have a geometra check the official use.
Bedrooms are prone to condensation and mould behind beds and wardrobes.
Look behind the bed and in wardrobes | Check window and ventilation | Notice musty smell
Official bedrooms need a minimum area and a window (usually 9 m² single, 14 m² double).
Measure the room | Check for a window to the outside | Compare with the floor plan
Room without window or too small, \'bedroom\' is officially storage.
Check each wall of this room separately for damp, salts and mould.
Look at the base and corners of each wall | Notice stains around windows | Measure if possible and record in the moisture module
Record cracks in walls and ceiling of this room.
Inspect walls and ceiling with raking light | Notice corners of windows and doors | Record cracks in the crack module
Cracks with offset or fresh edges.
Crack width alone is not enough to judge severity.
Check flatness, loose tiles and rot in the floor.
Place a marble on the floor | Tap the tiles | Look for wear and stains
Ceilings reveal leaks from above and sagging.
Inspect the ceiling with raking light | Look for rings, cracks and sagging | Look at the beams
Check the windows of this room for glazing, operation and damp.
Open and close each window | Check single or double glazing | Notice damp in the reveal
Count sockets and look at switches and lights.
Count sockets | Notice damaged or discoloured parts | Try the lighting
Do not open sockets or switches.
Is this room heated and does the radiator or stove work?
Check for a heat source | Ask whether it works | Notice leaks and rust
Add a radiator or other source.
In the cellar you often see the real structure and foundations.
Inspect walls, vaults and beams (only where safe) | Look for cracks, rust and rot | Look for props
Do not enter cellars with unstable stairs or ceilings.
With props or large cracks: engineer.
A cellar (cantina) usually may not officially be used as living space.
Ask how the cellar is used | Compare with the floor plan | Notice a kitchen or bedroom in the cellar
Used as storage according to plan.
Cellar used as living space without permit.
A cellar needs vents to remove moisture.
Look for vents or windows | Measure humidity | Notice rust and mould
Garages were often built later, sometimes with asbestos roofs or without permits.
Inspect roof, walls and floor | Notice corrugated sheets (possible asbestos) | Ask about the permit
Do not touch suspicious corrugated sheets.
Many old garages are too small or hard to reach for modern cars.
Measure width, length and door opening | Look at the slope and turning space of the drive | Ask whether it is private or shared
Car does not fit, drive unusable in winter.
Attic: roof timbers and underside of the roof
In the attic you see beams, purlins and the underside of the roof.
Use a torch on beams and boarding | Look for water rings, daylight and rot | Notice woodworm
Wet spots, daylight through tiles, rot, wood dust.
Rotten or broken beams, lots of daylight.
Only enter the attic via safe stairs and walk only on a solid floor, never on joists or ceiling boards.
With affected roof timbers: carpenter or engineer.
A well-insulated and ventilated attic prevents heat loss and condensation.
Check whether there is insulation and how thick | Notice wet or dirty insulation | Look for vents
No or wet insulation, condensation on timber.
Only enter the attic via safe stairs and walk only on a solid floor, never on joists or ceiling boards.
Martens, rats, bats or wasps often nest in attics.
Look for droppings, nests and gnawing | Notice damaged insulation and cables | Ask about pests
Only enter the attic via safe stairs and walk only on a solid floor, never on joists or ceiling boards.
Attics furnished as bedrooms are often not officially habitable (sottotetto non abitabile).
Measure the average height | Ask whether the conversion was permitted | Compare with the floor plan
Have a geometra check the status.
A large, overgrown garden costs time and money.
Walk through the garden | Notice overgrowth, dead trees and rubbish | Ask about irrigation and wells
Dead or leaning trees close to the house.
Can the plot be (partly) fenced, for instance for dogs?
Look at existing fences and walls | Ask whether fencing is allowed | Notice gaps and slopes
Fencing impossible because of terrain or rules.
A private well or rainwater storage is valuable in dry summers.
Ask about wells, cisterns and irrigation | Ask about permits and water quality | Notice open wells (fall hazard)
Do not go near open wells.
Terraces over living spaces often leak; also check the ceiling below.
Look for puddles, loose tiles and cracks | Check outlets | Inspect the ceiling under the terrace
A railing must be solid and high enough (usually at least 1 m).
Measure the height | Push gently to feel stability | Notice rust at the fixings
Do not lean on a railing whose strength you do not know.
Canopies, verandas and enclosed terraces are often built without permits.
Look at pergolas, canopies and glass enclosures | Ask about permits | Compare with the floor plan
The underside of a balcony shows rusting reinforcement and cracks.
Look at the underside of the balcony | Look for rust stains and spalled concrete | Notice sagging
Do not step onto a balcony with visible slab damage.
A balcony needs a safe railing and good drainage.
Measure and gently test the railing | Look at falls and outlet | Notice stains on the facade below
Loose railing, puddles, streaks on the facade.
Wobbly railing, water running to the wall.
Cadastral boundaries in rural areas often differ from fences and walls.
Ask the agent to point out the boundaries | Compare with the cadastral map (estratto di mappa) | Notice neighbours\' paths across the plot
Fences on someone else\'s land, dispute with neighbours.
Others may have a right of way, water pipe or cables across the plot (servitù).
Ask about servitù | Notice pipes, poles and paths | Have the notary check the deed
Paths, poles, wells of third parties.
Large trees can damage foundations, block gutters or fall.
Estimate the distance of large trees to the house | Notice leaning trees and dead branches | Look at roots near walls
Trees within a few metres, dead branches.
Leaning or dead trees towards the house.
Prune or have an arborist assess.
Barns, stables and rustici are often dilapidated or unregistered.
Inspect each outbuilding from outside | Ask whether it is registered in the cadastre | Notice asbestos and collapse risk
Corrugated sheets, water tanks and pipes from before 1992 may contain asbestos (eternit).
Look for corrugated sheets, old water tanks and flue pipes | Ask whether asbestos was removed | Note location and area
Have it tested and removed by a licensed company.
Never touch, break or drill suspicious materials.
Retaining walls hold back soil; a failing wall is dangerous and costly.
Inspect retaining walls from a distance | Notice bulging, cracks and loose stones | Check whether the wall leans
Repair or new wall by a specialist.
Do not walk on steep, wet or unstable slopes and do not stand below overhanging walls or rocks.
With bulging or leaning: geologist or engineer.
Retaining walls need openings to let water through; otherwise pressure builds up.
Look for weep holes at the base | See whether they drain or are blocked | Notice wet patches on the wall
Ownership and maintenance of retaining walls
Who must maintain a retaining wall is not always clear; that can become expensive.
Ask who owns each retaining wall | Ask about recent repairs | See whether the wall supports the road or neighbours
Walls on the boundary or along the road.
Unclear ownership of a poor wall.
Old terraces with dry-stone walls need a lot of maintenance.
Walk (safely) along the terraces | Count collapsed sections | Ask about maintenance
Collapsed sections, vegetation in the walls.
Do not walk on steep, wet or unstable slopes and do not stand below overhanging walls or rocks.
In mountain areas many places are flagged on PAI maps as landslide hazard zones.
Look for leaning trees, poles and cracks in the road | Ask about frane in the area | Ask the municipality about the PAI classification
Leaning trees and poles, cracked roads, bulges.
Do not walk on steep, wet or unstable slopes and do not stand below overhanging walls or rocks.
Rock faces above the house can drop stones.
Look at rock faces and loose stones above the house | Look for fallen stones and fence damage | Ask about protection nets
Do not walk on steep, wet or unstable slopes and do not stand below overhanging walls or rocks.
Position of the house on the slope
A house built into the slope often has damp on the uphill side.
See which walls are against the ground | Check those walls inside for damp | Look at orientation (sun)
Walls against the ground, north facing.
Drainage and waterproofing on the uphill side.
In higher mountain villages snow load on the roof and avalanche risk matter.
Ask how much snow normally falls | Look for snow guards on the roof | Ask about municipal avalanche maps
No snow guards, steep slopes above.
Roof designed for snow, no avalanche zone.
Do not walk on steep, wet or unstable slopes and do not stand below overhanging walls or rocks.
Rainwater running off the slope washes away soil and can flow against the house.
Look for gullies and washed-out soil | See where water flows in rain | Notice mud against walls
Water should flow away from the house, not towards it.
Look at the ground fall around the house | Look for puddles against the facade | Check for a drain channel or gravel strip
Puddles, ground higher than the floor.
Ground falls away from the house.
Houses near rivers or in low areas can be in a flood zone (PAI/PGRA).
Look at streams and rivers nearby | Ask about past floods | Ask the municipality about the hazard map
Water marks on walls, proximity to water.
House in high-risk zone, previous flooding.
Ditches, culverts and channels on the plot
Blocked ditches and culverts cause flooding in heavy rain.
Follow ditches and channels across the plot | Check that culverts under paths are open | Notice silt deposits
Natural springs or seepage on the plot can keep cellars and walls wet.
Look for wet patches that never seem to dry | Ask about springs | Notice rushes and moss in dry periods
Water emerging from the slope near the house.
A poor or private access road can cause problems all year round.
Drive or walk the last kilometres | Notice width, surface and steepness | Ask who maintains the road
Is the road cleared and gritted in winter?
Ask whether the municipality clears snow up to the house | Notice shady, steep stretches | Ask how often the road is closed
Steep shady stretches, no snow clearing.
Municipality clears up to the house.
Can ambulance, fire brigade and waste collection reach the house?
See whether a large vehicle can turn | Ask the distance to hospital and fire station | Notice bridges with weight limits
In village centres parking near the house is often impossible.
See where you can park | Ask about private spaces or permits | Measure the distance to the front door
Rent or buy a parking space.
Many steps to and inside the house are difficult with shopping, children or later in life.
Count the steps to the front door | Look at steep internal stairs | Think about future mobility
Only reachable via long, steep stairs.
Without a car: is there a bus or train within reasonable distance?
Find the nearest bus stop and station in the maps app | Ask how often the bus runs | Notice school buses
Can lorries for removals, fuel (LPG/wood) and renovation reach the house?
Ask how fuel is delivered | Look at clearance height and bends | Ask whether building materials have been delivered before
Account for it in the budget.
Roads, railways, factories, dogs or church bells can be very noisy.
Stand still for a few minutes inside and outside | Notice traffic, dogs and machines | Consider returning at another time
No fix; visit again at another time.
Livestock farms, sewage works or composting plants can cause bad smells.
Notice smells on arrival | Look for barns and plants nearby | Ask about manure spreading
How close are the neighbours and can they see into the garden or house?
Look at overlooking from neighbouring houses | Ask whether neighbouring houses are occupied | Notice neglected buildings next door
Derelict neighbouring building at risk of collapse.
In mountain valleys the sun can stay behind the mountains for weeks in winter.
Use the compass app to find the orientation of living room and garden | Ask how much sun there is in winter | Judge the view
North facing, mountains to the south.
Planned roads, wind turbines, solar farms or buildings can change the area.
Ask the municipality about the zoning plan (PRG/PGT) | Ask about planned projects | Notice construction signs nearby
Wild boar, wolves and hunting are normal in rural Italy.
Ask about hunting around the plot | Look for wild boar signs (rooted soil) | Ask about wolves if you have dogs or livestock
Hunting up to the house, much damage.
Houses surrounded by woodland or scrub have fire risk in dry summers.
See how close woodland or scrub is to the house | Ask about past fires | Ask about mandatory firebreaks
Scrub against the house, dry grass.
Recently burnt area, dense woodland against the house.
Large parts of Italy are seismic zones; older houses are often not earthquake resistant.
Ask the municipality\'s seismic zone (1–4) | Ask about strengthening (miglioramento sismico) | Notice iron tie plates on the facade
Have an engineer assess seismic vulnerability.
How far is the nearest supermarket, bakery and pharmacy?
Look them up in the maps app from the house | Ask about off-season opening hours | Note the actual route
Everything far or only open in summer.
Distance to medical care matters, especially in the countryside.
Find the nearest GP, A&E and vet | Ask how long an ambulance takes | Note the travel time
Are there schools nearby and is there a school bus?
Find schools in the maps app | Ask about school buses | Ask whether the village school stays open
Is the house connected to mains water, sewer, electricity and gas, or dependent on well, septic tank and LPG?
Ask about each utility | Ask about supplier and costs | Look at the meters
In the countryside you sometimes have to take waste to a collection point yourself.
Ask how waste is collected | Ask about TARI (waste tax) | Find the nearest collection point
Fibre or FWA is not available everywhere; remote work depends on it.
Ask which connection exists now | Check coverage per address with providers | Look at cables or antennas on the house
A test on site says more than a coverage map.
Run a speed test on your phone inside and outside | Note download, upload and ping | If possible test the house\'s Wi-Fi too
Satellite internet needs a clear view of the sky, often towards the north.
Look for a spot with a clear view of the sky | Notice trees and mountains | Ask whether a dish on the roof is allowed
In mountain villages and thick stone houses reception is often poor.
Check signal bars in different rooms | Make a test call | Note the provider
Mobile data can be an alternative to fixed internet.
Check whether you have 4G or 5G | Run a speed test on mobile data | Try several providers if you have them
The cadastral floor plan (planimetria catastale) must match the actual layout.
Request the planimetria | Walk the rooms with the plan in hand | Note differences (walls, windows, extensions)
Cadastral conformity is not the same as planning conformity; both must be correct.
Ask for the building permits (licenze, concessioni, permessi) | Ask whether a geometra has checked conformity | Ask about condoni or sanatorie
Abusi edilizi that cannot be legalised.
Have a geometra check the municipal records (accesso agli atti).
Always have a geometra or architect check before the compromesso.
The agibilità confirms the building is safe and habitable.
Ask whether there is a certificato/segnalazione di agibilità | See whether it was renewed after works | Ask the geometra what is missing
The APE is required for sale and gives the energy class.
Request the APE | Check it is valid (10 years) | Compare the class with what you see
Conformity declarations (dichiarazione di conformità, DM 37/08) for electrics, gas and heating.
Ask for certificates per system | Ask for the boiler logbook (libretto di impianto) | Check the latest inspection
No certificate for a gas installation.
Recent renovations (roof, systems) reduce risk; ask for proof.
Ask which works were done and when | Ask for invoices and warranties | Ask whether bonuses (Superbonus) were used
Superbonus works still subject to checks.
All owners must sign; with inheritances that can be many people.
Ask who the owners are | Ask about the deed of origin (atto di provenienza) | Ask whether a successione has been completed
There may be mortgages, liens or other charges on the house (ipoteche, pignoramenti).
Ask whether there are mortgages or liens | Have the notary do a visura ipotecaria | Ask how they will be cancelled at completion
Landscape, historic or hydrogeological vincoli restrict alterations.
Ask about landscape, historic or hydrogeological vincoli | Ask the municipality for a CDU (certificato di destinazione urbanistica) for land | Ask what this means for your plans
Vincoli that make your plans impossible.
Apartments and shared buildings have joint costs and decisions.
Ask for the regulations and annual costs | Ask whether works have been approved (lavori deliberati) | Ask about arrears
Major approved works payable by buyer.
Request a statement from the amministratore.
A rented house or leased land cannot always be handed over vacant.
Ask whether house or land is rented or leased | Ask about contracts and end dates | Ask about pre-emption rights (prelazione)
Running contract or farmer\'s pre-emption right.
The compromesso binds both parties; the deposit (caparra) can be lost.
Ask for a draft before signing | Have your own adviser review it | Include conditions (mortgage, conformity)
Seller or agent in a hurry.
Have a lawyer or notary review.
Sign nothing before your own adviser has read it.
In Italy buyers usually also pay agency fees (3–4% + VAT) and notary and registration costs.
Ask for the fee in writing | Ask for an estimate of notary and taxes | Check the agent is registered (REA)
Agricultural land around the house has different rules and taxes; building is often not allowed.
Ask which parcels are included | Ask the zoning per parcel (CDU) | Ask about subsidies or obligations
Parcels not in the deed or zoned differently.
